claims.text: High-temperature in situ synthesis of near-equiatomic PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles produces near-equilibrium atomic distributions.
High-temperature synthesized PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles have lower defect densities than particles made by low-temperature colloidal reduction.
A near-equilibrium, low-defect state enhances structural and chemical stability during high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric service.
High-temperature synthesis provides greater precursor or atomic mobility than low-temperature synthesis.
Low-temperature solution-based synthesis inhibits precursor mobility and can kinetically trap the resulting nanoparticles.
Low-temperature colloidal reduction necessarily produces defect-rich PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles.
The synthesis routes can be compared under catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric testing at 473–1923 K.
Matching particle-size distributions and purity levels is part of the proposed controlled comparison.
The principal structural mediator is atomic ordering and defect density rather than synthesis route acting through some other route-dependent property.
Sufficient atomic mobility during high-temperature synthesis minimizes defects.
High-temperature processing can produce a single-phase or uniform multielement distribution.
Defect minimization and uniform elemental distribution reduce local energy fluctuations.
Reduced local energy fluctuations suppress phase segregation and coarsening during high-temperature service.
Defects and local chemical inhomogeneities in kinetically trapped nanoparticles act as nuclei for degradation under thermal cycling.
High-temperature synthesized particles will show less coarsening and phase segregation than low-temperature synthesized particles under identical service conditions.
High-temperature synthesized particles will retain catalytic and thermoelectric performance better than the low-temperature baseline.
The proposed mechanism remains applicable to PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles throughout 773–1173 K catalytic service and 473–1923 K thermoelectric service.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes stability to a near-equilibrium state created by high mobility, whereas PMC7069714 reports that sluggish diffusion and high barriers preserve uniformity and that a fully diffusion-equilibrated nanoparticle segregates.

The low-temperature route is characterized as intrinsically defective and degradation-prone, but PMC10621632 reports that inhibited precursor mobility at low temperature favors formation of a single-phase HEA nanoparticle.

The hypothesis assumes that a near-equiatomic equilibrium configuration is stabilizing, while PMC10056590 reports precipitation after near-equilibrium slow cooling and argues that optimal phase stability in its different alloy system is non-equiatomic.
